answers.answer:
Short answer: SCOPe classifies by evolutionary unit and fold, not by length. All three domains are built from the same homologous ~33-35-residue TAL repeat, and SCOPe treats an entire tandem array of such repeats as one domain, so a fragment with ~1.5 repeats and a construct with ~20 repeats land in the same family. Length differences here reflect how many copies of the repeat the deposited construct contains, not a difference in evolutionary origin.

What the current release (SCOPe 2.08, stable; latest periodic update 2.08-2026-08-16) records:
- Family a.298.1.1 'TAL (transcription activator-like) effector' (sunid 267609) sits under superfamily a.298.1 'TAL effector-like' (sunid 267596), fold a.298 'Left-handed alpha-alpha superhelix' (sunid 267589), class a (all-alpha, sunid 46456).
- d2kq5a_ (sunid 264989): protein PthA, species Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. citri [TaxId 92829]; domain = 2kq5 chain A, 51 residues (SEQRES). This is the NMR structure of a PthA fragment covering roughly one and a half repeats (EQVVAIASNIGGKQALETVQRLLPVLCQAHGLTPEQVVAIASHDGGKQALE).
- d3v6pa_ (sunid 265556): protein dHax3, species Xanthomonas [TaxId 338]; domain = 3v6p chain A, 373 residues, i.e. ~11.5 tandem repeats of the canonical 34-residue unit (LTPxQVVAIASxxGGKQALETVQRLLPVLCQAHG). 3v6p is the DNA-free crystal structure of the engineered dHax3 repeat array.
- d4cj9a_ (sunid 265996): protein BurrH, species Burkholderia rhizoxinica [TaxId 412963]; domain = 4cj9 chain A, 752 residues, ~19.5 repeats plus the N-terminal capping segment. BurrH is a TALE-like protein from Burkholderia whose repeats are more divergent from the Xanthomonas repeats (roughly 35-40% identity per repeat) but still clearly homologous.

Why one family is justified at each level of the hierarchy:
- Family (a.298.1.1) is the level of clear sequence-based homology. The repeat units of PthA, dHax3 and BurrH align end to end with conserved positions (the ~34-residue two-helix hairpin, the glycine-rich loop, the repeat-variable diresidue at positions 12-13). The 51-residue PthA fragment is essentially identical in sequence to individual dHax3 repeats, so family membership for d2kq5a_ rests on sequence identity of the repeat unit, not on the fragment having the full superhelix. SCOPe places each distinct protein (PthA, dHax3, BurrH) as a separate protein node under the family, with the species nodes below them, which is exactly how the API represents them.
- Superfamily (a.298.1) is the probable-common-ancestry level. In 2.08 the 'TAL effector-like' superfamily contains only this one family, so family and superfamily are currently coextensive; the superfamily node exists to accommodate more divergent TALE-like repeat proteins later, not because the three domains differ in confidence of homology.
- Fold (a.298, left-handed alpha-alpha superhelix) describes only geometry: tandem two-helix hairpins packed into a left-handed solenoid. Fold-level similarity to other solenoid folds is not evidence of homology and should not be used to infer common ancestry with unrelated superhelical proteins.
- Class a just says all-alpha.

Why the lengths differ so much: SCOPe domain boundaries follow the observed polypeptide in the PDB entry. 2kq5 was an NMR study of a minimal fragment; 3v6p is an engineered 11.5-repeat construct made for crystallography; 4cj9 is a near-full-length natural BurrH repeat array. Because the TAL repeat domain is a solenoid with no fixed repeat count (natural TALEs range from a handful to >30 repeats), SCOPe does not split the array into per-repeat domains, and does not create different families for different repeat counts. Repeat copy number is a property of the construct or the gene, not a classification criterion.

Important limits:
- Homology/function transfer: family membership tells you the repeats share ancestry and the general DNA-binding mode (one repeat per base, specificity set by the repeat-variable diresidue). It does not transfer DNA target specificity between PthA, dHax3 and BurrH, because that depends on the specific RVD sequence of each array, which differs. BurrH also uses a partly different RVD code than Xanthomonas TALEs, so even RVD-based predictions must be made per protein, with experimental binding data, not inherited from the family label.
- Template use: d2kq5a_ is a 1.5-repeat fragment and does not display the superhelical pitch or curvature of a full array; it is a suitable template for a single repeat hairpin only. d3v6pa_ is DNA-free and the array is more extended than the DNA-bound state (compare the DNA-bound 3v6t); d4cj9a_ has a different repeat count and a divergent sequence. None of the three is a drop-in whole-length template for another; repeat-level modeling plus knowledge of the bound/unbound superhelical state is required.
- Representative selection: if one picks a single representative for a.298.1.1 (e.g. by ASTRAL sequence-identity filtering), the choice of a 51-, 373- or 752-residue domain strongly changes what structural information is captured, so the family's length heterogeneity should be considered explicitly when building non-redundant sets.
- Release specificity: the sunids, protein/species node layout and the single-family superfamily are as recorded in SCOPe 2.08; the TAL effector family did not exist in SCOP 1.75 and may be reorganized in later releases.
evidence_used: pretrained knowledge of TAL effector repeat structure (2kq5, 3v6p/3v6t, 4cj9 literature)
